newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communist leader goes on offensive against Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Communist leader goes on offensive against Yeltsin.

text.p: Opposition communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, returning to the offensive against Boris Yeltsin, said on Thursday he doubted the president would be able to rule Russia properly when he recovers from heart surgery.

Zyuganov, who has largely held his fire since Yeltsin's quintuple bypass operation, went on the attack one day after the president was shown on Russian television for the first time since the surgery.

"Anyone who knows anything about medicine knows that after three heart attacks, five bypasses and with concerns about a number of other organs, a person can not work at full strength," Zyuganov told reporters.

"They talk now about 'ability to work'? What is this? Some think 30 minutes in enough, others an hour. I think that in crisis situations a person should work for 24 hours, take control of the situation and be able to take urgent decisions."
Zyuganov, talking to reporters in his office in the lower house of parliament, said Yeltsin had not been able to answer vital questions about how to solve Russia's problems even before he fell ill.
"Even when Mr Yeltsin was in good, sporty form and completely healthy, I did not hear answers to the questions on these problems," he said.
Russian television showed the 65-year-old president walking slowly through the grounds of Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital with his family on Wednesday.
Yeltsin spoke clearly in the footage and said he was in fighting form, making clear he was keen to get back to work.

Doctors have said the workaholic president, who has often surprised critics with his political comebacks, may be back in the Kremlin by the end of the year. They have suggested that he should have no problems working about eight or 10 hours a day.

Zyuganov, who was defeated by Yeltsin in last July's presidential election run-off, has continued to criticise Yeltsin during his illness, but less fiercely than in the past. This was apparently out of respect for his health problems.
But redoubling his attacks on Thursday, he said Russia was in chaos, ran a risk of becoming a dictatorship and could face a rebellion by people fed up with economic hardships.
"When times are bad for women and children in Russian history, it is open to mass, fierce protests, even to the point of rebellion," the 52-year-old communist said.
"Chaos can, in any case, end in tough, dictatorial authorities," he said.

Zyuganov reiterated concern at the powers which he said Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais had amassed since Yeltsin fell ill just before his re-election. "Today there are attempts to impose a regency under Chubais and company," he said.

Despite his opposition to Yeltsin, Zyuganov made clear that he wanted to avert civil strife violence over Russia's economic problems and repeated that the best way forward was through cooperation, dialogue and national reconcilation.
